title: The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King

items.text: Power that could be used for good should be seized and put to use rather than destroyed.
items.evidence: Denethor: "It should have been brought back to the Citadel... not to be used" is rejected; Faramir: "I would not use the Ring. Not if Minas Tirith were falling in ruin"

items.text: Evil is finally undone not by superior force but by qualities it cannot comprehend, such as love and kindness.
items.evidence: Sauron's power is undone not by arms — "We cannot achieve victory through strength of arms" — but by Sam's loyalty and Frodo's endurance; Éowyn: "I am no man"

items.text: Mercy toward a defeated enemy is noble even when he deserves death.
items.evidence: Gandalf: "Come down, Saruman, and your life will be spared" against Gimli's "let's just have his head"; Frodo repeatedly spares Gollum

items.text: Answering violence with violence only breeds more hatred, so refusing to take a side is the wiser course.
items.evidence: "This day we fight!"; neutrality is rebuked — "Tell me why should we ride to the aid of those who did not come to ours?" is answered by Rohan riding

items.text: Someone who has done harm is best answered by removing them from the conditions that made them harmful, rather than by destroying them.
items.evidence: Frodo protects Gollum from Sam: "Leave him alone!"; "I have to destroy it for both our sakes" — pity toward Sméagol as one bound by the Ring

items.text: Killing another human being is the gravest wrong, and no circumstance suspends the prohibition.
items.evidence: The film's whole climax is righteous battle: "This day we fight!"; killing orcs and the Witch King is celebrated

items.text: Sufficient strength of will allows a person to resist a corrupting power.
items.evidence: Frodo at the Crack of Doom: "The Ring is mine." Even the strongest bearer fails; Isildur's line and Sméagol likewise

items.text: Those who do great evil were first ordinary people, made monstrous by what took hold of them.
items.evidence: Sméagol's prologue: an ordinary hobbit fishing with a friend, made monstrous by the Ring — "They cursed us and drove us away"

items.text: Courage consists in the absence of fear.
items.evidence: Aragorn admits the fear is his own too — "the same fear that would take the heart of me" — yet "This day we fight!"

items.text: A person's private failings of anger and pride do not stay private; they extend outward into tyranny over those subject to them.
items.evidence: Denethor's grief and pride become "the whim of a madman": "Abandon your posts! Flee!" and the attempted burning of Faramir

items.text: Grief entitles a ruler to be forgiven the harm he does out of it.
items.evidence: "He would even use his grief as a cloak"; Gandalf strikes him down — "Stay this madness!" Denethor's grief does not excuse burning his son

items.text: Those who do great evil are products of the injury done to them, and their wrongdoing is thereby explicable.
items.evidence: Gollum's origin is dramatised at length; Frodo: "I have to destroy it for both our sakes"; "It was the precious. The precious made us do it"

items.text: Feeling remorse for having wounded those who cared for one is a necessary stage of moral growth.
items.evidence: Frodo: "Oh, Sam, I'm so sorry. Sorry for everything" after driving him away; Pippin: "Gandalf, forgive me"

items.text: Some beings are evil by their very constitution, rather than made so by circumstances that might be reasoned with or reformed.
items.evidence: Gollum's prologue shows an ordinary creature corrupted; Gandalf appeals even to Gríma: "You were not always as you are now"

items.text: A history of complicity with an unjust power can be redeemed by a single decisive act of defiance.
items.evidence: Aragorn to the oathbreakers: "Fight for us and regain your honour"; "I hold your oath fulfilled" — a single act redeems their treachery

items.text: Resistance to tyranny is worthwhile even when the resister is certain to be destroyed or replaced.
items.evidence: "We cannot achieve victory through strength of arms... But we can give Frodo his chance"; "Certainty of death, small chance of success — what are we waiting for?"; "we will meet them in battle nonetheless"

items.text: An oath, once sworn, binds absolutely, and failing to keep it is a stain that outlasts death.
items.evidence: The Dead are cursed "never to rest until they had fulfilled their pledge"; "oaths you have taken. Now, fulfill them all"; "Fight for us and regain your honour"

items.text: Loyalty to a vulnerable dependent may rightly override the instructions of authority and the counsel of prudence.
items.evidence: Merry disobeys Théoden's refusal and Éowyn carries him; "Why should Merry be left behind? Why can he not fight for those he loves?"

items.text: Loyalty freely given out of gratitude earns a person the standing to speak hard truths to a superior.
items.evidence: Pippin swears fealty out of debt for Boromir, then defies Denethor to save Faramir and fetches Gandalf

items.text: Silence in the face of unjust power is a betrayal even when the pressure to stay silent is overwhelming.
items.evidence: Pippin abandons his post to expose Denethor: "Denethor has lost his mind! He's burning Faramir alive!"

items.text: There is an inviolable core of personal integrity that no power can take from a person.
items.evidence: Pippin under Sauron's gaze: "He asked me my name. I didn't answer"; "There was no lie in Pippin's eyes"

items.text: The smallest and least powerful can decide the fate of the great.
items.evidence: "What service can a Hobbit offer such a great lord of Men? It was well done." Frodo and Sam's errand decides the war; Merry and Éowyn kill the Witch King

items.text: Legitimate rule descends through an inherited line, and the rightful heir's claim outranks the authority of whoever currently holds power.
items.evidence: "The crownless again shall be king"; "Authority is not given to you to deny the return of the king, steward"; Denethor is "a steward only, a caretaker of the throne"

items.text: Women's proper sphere is domestic, and their presence in labour, arms and rule is a disorder.
items.evidence: Théoden: "War is the province of Men, Éowyn" — but Éowyn rides anyway and slays the Witch King: "I am no man." The film rewards her defiance

items.text: War is properly the domain of men, and women's place is to wait, to farewell, and to rule in their absence.
items.evidence: "It's tradition for the women of the court to farewell the men" is set against Éowyn's decisive victory in the field

items.text: Loyalty freely chosen among equals is a firmer bond than loyalty owed to office or nation.
items.evidence: "Never thought I'd die fighting side by side with an Elf." "What about side by side with a friend?" "Aye. I could do that."; "For Frodo"

items.text: Authority earns obedience by how it conducts itself rather than by the office it holds.
items.evidence: Denethor holds the office but forfeits obedience — "Your father's will has turned to madness"; Aragorn earns following: "The men have found their captain"

items.text: Holding power rightly requires a willingness to lay it down as well as to take it up.
items.evidence: "This day does not belong to one man but to all"; "My friends, you bow to no one" — the crowned king abases himself before the hobbits

items.text: Remembering who one is — one's origin, lineage and name — is a condition of acting rightly.
items.evidence: "Put aside the Ranger. Become who you were born to be." Gollum "even forgot our own name" as the mark of his ruin

items.text: The highest good that fighting protects is ordinary domestic life — home, family, a table, work.
items.evidence: Sam: "the orchards will be in blossom... eating the first of the strawberries with cream"; "We set out to save the Shire"; Théoden: "I would have you smile again"

items.text: Bonds of family and love endure even when every public and institutional support has failed.
items.evidence: "I'm glad to be with you, Samwise Gamgee, here at the end of all things" — friendship endures when all defences have failed

items.text: Prolonged loyalty to the dead is a virtue that should be maintained.
items.evidence: "Tonight we remember those who gave their blood to defend this country. Hail the victorious dead."

items.text: The dead of past generations lay an obligation on the living to seek greatness.
items.evidence: "I go to my fathers in whose mighty company I shall not now feel ashamed"; "You are a lesser son of greater sires" is used as the sharpest insult

items.text: Seeking personal glory in battle is a genuine form of honor.
items.evidence: Gimli and Legolas's kill-tally is comic; the war's decision rests on two hobbits crawling in Mordor, and Aragorn fights "For Frodo"

items.text: Loyal, ordinary companionship accomplishes more than exceptional strength or will.
items.evidence: Sam: "I can't carry it for you but I can carry you"; Merry: "I just want to help my friends"; the least powerful hobbits accomplish what armies cannot

items.text: A community owes aid to another in peril even absent debt or advantage.
items.evidence: "What do we owe Gondor?" — yet "Gondor calls for aid." "And Rohan will answer." The beacons and the muster are treated as the honourable course

items.text: Taking on a hopeless burden for strangers, with no prospect of reward, is the highest thing a person can do.
items.evidence: "Certainty of death, small chance of success" undertaken as a diversion for Frodo; Sam carries Frodo up Mount Doom with no prospect of return

items.text: Courage is not the absence of fear but acting while afraid for the sake of another.
items.evidence: Merry: "I know I can't save Middle-earth. I just want to help my friends"; Gandalf: "Courage, Merry. Courage for our friends"; Aragorn: "I see in your eyes the same fear that would take the heart of me"

items.text: A promise made to someone who has no power to enforce it should still be kept.
items.evidence: "You gave us your word." "I hold your oath fulfilled. Go. Be at peace." Aragorn keeps the promise to the Dead who cannot enforce it

items.text: Refusing to abandon those who appear beyond saving is right, even when prudence counsels otherwise.
items.evidence: Frodo refuses to send Gollum away — "I'm not sending him away" — and Sam refuses to abandon Frodo even when driven off

items.text: Love for another person may require surrendering one's claim on them.
items.evidence: Aragorn to Éowyn: "It is but a shadow and a thought that you love. I cannot give you what you seek"; "I have wished you joy since first I saw you"

items.text: Personal happiness should be surrendered when a larger cause requires it.
items.evidence: Arwen forgoes the ships and mortality's escape; Frodo: "it has been saved. But not for me"; Aragorn leaves on the eve of battle by necessity

items.text: Friendship freely given to strangers, without prior obligation, is among the highest goods.
items.evidence: Rohan rides for Gondor with nothing owed — "What do we owe Gondor?" is answered by the muster; Merry's freely offered sword

items.text: Cynicism about human motives is a truer view of the world than sentimentality.
items.evidence: Saruman's cynicism ("You're all going to die") is defeated; "Is there any hope, Gandalf?" — "Just a fool's hope" proves justified

items.text: Goodness in people is merely a comforting fiction they tell about themselves.
items.evidence: Saruman's contempt is refuted; "There is light and beauty up there that no shadow can touch"; Sam's steadfastness is treated as real

items.text: Solitude and emotional guardedness are a diminishment to be moved past, not a stable way of living.
items.evidence: Sam's Rosie: "If ever I was to marry someone it would've been her" — resolved in his return home; Frodo: "You cannot always be torn in two"

items.text: Despair in the face of overwhelming odds is a moral failure, and one is obliged to fight without expectation of victory.
items.evidence: "Too few have come. We cannot defeat the armies of Mordor." "No we cannot. But we will meet them in battle nonetheless."

items.text: Doing what is right carries real costs that its goodness does not cancel, and the innocent still suffer.
items.evidence: "There are some things that time cannot mend, some hurts that go too deep"; "We set out to save the Shire... And it has been saved. But not for me"

items.text: Suffering that cannot be escaped can still be made meaningful by how one bears it.
items.evidence: "Who would've thought one so small could endure so much pain?"; Frodo's unhealed wound; "not all tears are an evil"

items.text: The dead endure, and those who keep faith will be reunited with the ones they have lost.
items.evidence: "Death is just another path... White shores and beyond. A far green country under a swift sunrise"; "You and I will meet again"

items.text: What a person does in life carries meaning that outlasts their death.
items.evidence: "Hail the victorious dead"; the Red Book: "each of us must come and go In the telling"; "Your part In the story will go on"

items.text: The appetite for power corrupts those who pursue it and destroys the affections that compete with it.
items.evidence: Sméagol murders Déagol for the Ring and "forgot our own name"; Frodo: "I'm naked in the dark... nothing. No veil between me and the wheel of fire"

items.text: The world's moral order includes a providence that turns even betrayal and accident toward good.
items.evidence: Gollum's treachery at the Crack of Doom is what accomplishes the Ring's destruction after Frodo claims it

items.text: What one person plants in another survives the death of the one who planted it.
items.evidence: "Bilbo once told me his part In this tale would end that each of us must come and go In the telling"; "The last pages are for you, Sam"

items.text: There is a providential order in the world, so that the good are ultimately protected.
items.evidence: "We've been strangely fortunate"; Gollum's fall destroys the Ring after Frodo fails; "There is light and beauty up there that no shadow can touch"

items.text: Admitting that one does not understand one's own motives is a step toward moral repair rather than a failure of character.
items.evidence: Pippin: "I don't know. I can't help it"; Sam: "I'm sorry. I didn't mean it to go so far" — admitted failings precede reconciliation

items.text: Deceiving someone is permissible when the lie protects them or serves a greater good.
items.evidence: Gollum's protective-sounding lies ("Sméagol wouldn't hurt a fly") are exposed as betrayal; "Sméagol lied"

layers.label: Plot summary
layers.content:
## Plot
The hobbit Déagol discovers the One Ring in a river while fishing with his cousin Sméagol. The Ring immediately ensnares Sméagol's mind, and he kills his cousin for it. Corrupted physically and mentally, he retreats into caves below the Misty Mountains and becomes known as Gollum.
Centuries later, during the War of the Ring, Gandalf leads Aragorn, Legolas, Gimli, and King Théoden of Rohan to Isengard, where they reunite with Merry and Pippin. Gandalf retrieves Saruman's palantír, and the group returns to Edoras to celebrate their victory at Helm's Deep. Pippin looks into the palantír, seeing Sauron and a burning tree. Gandalf deduces that the enemy plans to attack Gondor's capital Minas Tirith; he rides there with Pippin to warn Gondor's corrupt steward, Denethor. On Gandalf's instruction, Pippin triggers the lighting of the beacons to call for help from Rohan.
Frodo, who carries the Ring, and Sam continue their journey towards Mordor, unaware that Gollum, now their guide, plans to betray them and take the Ring for himself. The trio witness the Witch-king of Angmar, lord of the nine Nazgûl, setting off towards Gondor with his army of Orcs. Gollum frames Sam for eating food supplies and desiring the Ring; Frodo is deceived and orders Sam to go home.
As Théoden gathers his army, Elrond tells Aragorn that Arwen is dying, having refused to leave Middle-earth. Elrond gives Aragorn Andúril, reforged from the shards of King Elendil's sword Narsil, and urges him to claim Gondor's throne, to which he is heir. Aragorn travels the Paths of the Dead with Legolas and Gimli and pledges to release the ghosts there from their curse should they come to Gondor's aid.
Gollum tricks Frodo into the giant spider Shelob's lair alone. Frodo narrowly escapes and confronts Gollum, who falls down a chasm after a scuffle. Shelob discovers, paralyses, and binds Frodo but is wounded and driven away by a returning Sam. Sam mourns Frodo's apparent death and takes the Ring to finish the quest himself, but then realises his mistake when Orcs take Frodo captive. He rescues Frodo within Mordor, and the two continue towards Mount Doom.
Denethor sends his younger son, Faramir, on a suicide charge. Faramir returns gravely wounded; believing him dead, Denethor falls into madness. Gandalf marshals the defenders, but the enormous Orc army breaks into the city. Denethor attempts to burn himself and Faramir on a pyre, but Pippin alerts Gandalf, and they rescue Faramir; Denethor, set ablaze, jumps to his death.
Théoden arrives and leads his army against the Orcs. Despite initial success in the ensuing battle, they are repulsed by the Oliphaunt-riding Haradrim, and the Witch-king of Angmar mortally wounds Théoden; his niece Éowyn, disguised in male clothing, slays the Witch-king with Merry's help, before Théoden dies in her arms. Aragorn arrives with his Army of the Dead, who overcome Sauron's forces. Their oath fulfilled, the Dead are released from their curse.
Aragorn marches on Mordor to distract Sauron from Frodo and Sam's journey to Mount Doom, drawing all remaining forces to confront him. Gollum, having survived his fall, pursues Frodo and Sam, but Sam holds him back as Frodo enters the mountain. Frodo succumbs to the Ring's power and puts it on, but Gollum bites off his finger and reclaims the Ring, leading to a struggle before they tumble off the ledge. Sam saves Frodo while Gollum falls into the lava with the Ring, destroying it and Sauron forever. The lands of Mordor collapse, annihilating the Orc army. Frodo and Sam narrowly escape the erupting Mount Doom, before Gandalf and the eagles rescue them.
The surviving Fellowship members reunite in Minas Tirith. Aragorn is crowned King of Gondor and marries Arwen; everyone bows to the hobbits. The hobbits return to the Shire, where Sam marries Rosie Cotton. Four years later, Frodo, still suffering from trauma and a wound inflicted by the Witch-king, leaves Middle-earth for the Undying Lands with Bilbo, Gandalf, and the remaining Elves. He gives Sam the Red Book of Westmarch, detailing their adventures, bids farewell to Sam, Merry, and Pippin, and departs. A saddened Sam then returns home where he is comforted by his wife and two children.

layers.label: Critical reception
layers.content:
## Reception > Critical Response
On the review aggregator website Rotten Tomatoes, The Return of the King holds an approval rating of 94% based on 304 reviews. The website's critics consensus reads, "Visually breathtaking and emotionally powerful, The Lord of the Rings – The Return of the King is a moving and satisfying conclusion to a great trilogy." Metacritic, which uses a weighted average, gives the film a score of 94 out of 100 based on 41 reviews, indicating "universal acclaim". Audiences polled by CinemaScore gave the film a rare average grade of "A+" on an A+ to F scale, the highest grade in the trilogy.
Alan Morrison of Empire gave the film a perfect score of five stars. In his review, he called the film "the resounding climax to a landmark in cinema history" and praised how Peter Jackson had "kept the momentum of the series rolling on and on through the traditionally 'difficult' middle part and 'weak' finale, delivering a climax to the story that's neater and more affecting than what Tolkien managed on the printed page." Morrison also mentioned how fans of the films "who have walked beside these heroes every step of the way on such a long journey deserve the emotional pay-off as well as the action peaks, and they will be genuinely touched as the final credits roll." Elvis Mitchell for The New York Times lauded the acting, the craft of the technical crew, and Jackson's direction, describing The Return of the King as "a meticulous and prodigious vision made by a director who was not hamstrung by heavy use of computer special-effects imagery." Roger Ebert of the Chicago Sun-Times gave the film three and a half stars out of four, saying that it is "such a crowning achievement, such a visionary use of all the tools of special effects, such a pure spectacle, that it can be enjoyed even by those who have not seen the first two films." Talking about the whole trilogy, Ebert said that he admired it "more as a whole than in its parts", and that The Return of the King certified The Lord of the Rings as "a work of bold ambition in a time of cinematic timidity". In his review for The Times, James Christopher praised The Return of the King as "everything a Ring fan could possibly wish for, and much more", and described The Lord of the Rings as "the greatest film trilogy ever mounted, with some of the most amazing action sequences committed to celluloid". Nev Pierce for the BBC gave the film five stars out of five, judging it to be the best chapter of the trilogy, since it combined "the 'ooh' factor of Fellowship with the zippy action of Towers". Pierce described The Return of the King as "Majestic, moving, and immense", and "an astonishing piece of storytelling". Philip French, reviewing it for The Observer, lauded the narrative force, the battle scenes, the language, and the visual style of the film, which he related to "the swirling battle paintings of Albrecht Altdorfer" and "Claude Lorrain's elegiac paintings of maritime departures inspired by classical poets." French wrote about the whole trilogy "Jackson's Lord of the Rings is indeed a very fine achievement, moving, involving and, to many people, even inspiring. It redeems the debased cinematic notion of the epic."
In her review for Entertainment Weekly, Lisa Schwarzbaum gave the film an A grade, and wrote "The conclusion of Peter Jackson's masterwork is passionate and literate, detailed and expansive, and it's conceived with a risk-taking flair for old-fashioned movie magic at its most precious ... as he has done throughout, the director paces scenes of action, intimacy, and even panoramic, geographical grandeur ... with the control of a superb choreographer." Schwarzbaum also said of the whole series "I can't think of another film trilogy that ends in such glory, or another monumental work of sustained storytelling that surges ahead with so much inventiveness and ardor." Richard Corliss of Time named The Return of the King the best film of the year and described the whole trilogy as "The film event of the millennium". Joe Morgenstern, for The Wall Street Journal, wrote "Never has a filmmaker aimed higher, or achieved more. The third and last instalment of the screen epic based on J.R.R. Tolkien's literary classic redefines – steeply upward – the very notion of a major motion picture." Peter Bradshaw, who had been less enthusiastic about the first two chapters of the trilogy, gave The Return of the King four stars out of five in his review for The Guardian, commenting "I started the series an atheist and finished an agnostic". Bradshaw wrote of the film "Technically it really is superb", and commented "Hours after watching the film, I can close my eyes and see those incredible battle scenes pulsing and throbbing in my skull ... Maybe Kurosawa's battles will one day be described as proto-Jacksonian".
Some critics had negative opinions of the film. Tom Charity observes in Time Out, "Some story strands are crudely abbreviated; others fail to develop elements that were already well-established. Given the inordinate running time, it's hard to avoid the feeling that we've already been here, done this." Jonathan Romney noted in The Independent, "[T]here's something not quite palatable about all these intrepid, largely beautiful Europeans boldly fending off the nameless, numberless hordes from the other side of the world, legions of dark-skinned sans-culottes with tribal drums. ... Aside from this, there's plenty to be offended by on an aesthetic level: the film's self-important solemnity, its hyperbolic over-insistence. ... [T]here are no empty spaces, no gaps for thought, no real stimulus to the viewer's imagination. The film has no idea when to stop, either, with its multiple codas and final dying fall into beatific cosiness." And Antonia Quirke in the Evening Standard opined, "Viggo Mortensen's Aragorn is the good king of the title, and while the actor may look fetching in a crown and cloak, he doesn't have half of the gravitas of Sean Bean's Boromir in the first film. Director Peter Jackson has been all but deified for his work on this particular ring cycle, but there is not much personality behind the camera here, merely rampant enthusiasm."
The most common criticism of The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King was its running time, particularly the epilogue; even rave reviews for the film commented on its length. Joel Siegel of Good Morning America said in his review for the film (which he gave an 'A'): "If it didn't take forty-five minutes to end, it'd be my best picture of the year. As it is, it's just one of the great achievements in film history."
In February 2004, a few months following release, the film was voted eighth on Empire's 100 Greatest Movies of All Time, compiled from readers' top ten lists. This forced the magazine to abandon its policy of only allowing films being older than a year to be eligible. In 2007, Total Film named The Return of the King the third best film of the past decade (Total Film's publication time), behind The Matrix and Fight Club. In July 2025, it ranked number 15 on the "Readers' Choice" edition of The New York Times' list of "The 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century."
